newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik soldiers die in clashes with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Tajik soldiers die in clashes with rebels.

text.p: Tajikistan's Islamist opposition said it had taken control of the town of Garm on Sunday after fierce clashes with Tajik government troops.

"Garm came under opposition control in the second half of the day," Jaloleddin Makhmudov, an opposition official and a member of a United Nations ceasefire commission based in the capital Dushanbe, told Reuters.

The Tajik government said four of its soldiers had been killed when opposition guerrillas stormed administrative buildings in Garm, some 200 km (130 miles) to the east of the capital of the former Soviet republic, on Sunday.
There was no word on opposition casualties.
"Full responsibility for this lies with the (Tajik) opposition," said a statement by the interior and security ministries issued to journalists.
U.N. observers said about 100 rebels had captured several administrative buildings in Garm and that fighting had been reported near the town's airport.
"There are unconfirmed reports of a large number of casualties and extensive destruction of buildings," the U.N. Mission of Observers to Tajikistan (UNMOT) said in a statement.
It also said that government helicopters and planes had attacked the town centre.
"The marked escalation of armed confrontation constitutes gross ceasefire violations, laden with tragic consequences," it said.
Fighting in the Central Asian state has intensified over the past month, despite a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire which is regularly flouted by both sides.
Tajik government troops, backed by the Russian military, have fought the Islamist opposition in the remote, impoverished republic bordering Afghanistan and China for nearly five years.
The guerrillas operate out of bases inside Afghanistan and control more than half the country, mainly sparsely populated mountainous territory in the east.
The fighting erupted just days before talks planned for December 9 between Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri in northern Afghanistan.
The opposition was widely held to have carried out attacks on Russian soldiers in the capital Dushanbe earlier this month.

A complex web of regional and clan rivalries underlies the struggle between the secular government and Islamist guerrillas in a bitter civil war which has killed tens of thousands and displaced many more among the population of 5.7 million.
